edges: Khosrova explains that the Church’s fasting rules fell very differently on south and north because of which fats each had.
The Council of Angers’s ban on butter is a Lenten fasting rule.
Brittany’s petition of 1491 was for exemption from the Lenten ban because it had no oil.
Tradition says the Butter Tower was paid for from butter dispensations, though no accounts survive.
Whale blubber, ‘Lenten fat’, was eaten on fast days, an outlet for the same fasting rules.
The whale taxes of 1197, 1261 and 1324 fall on the Basque and English whale fisheries.
Spanish oil sent north and oil as a currency are two faces of the oil trade of the high Middle Ages in the south.
The shift to cattle butter made butter common enough to pay for dispensations.
Tunisian oil imports into Egypt and Egypt’s linseed exports to Syria and Aden are the two directions of the same Mediterranean oil exchange in the Geniza.
Egypt’s own linseed and sesame oils filled out the olive oil imported from Tunisia.
The Chi le pien’s list of oils is Needham’s evidence for the Song oil trade that the seven-necessities passage describes.
The tallow-tree candles are one of the oils the Chi le pien lists.
Oil pressing establishments of Hangzhou and Wang Zhen’s press describe the same trade, though Needham says no Song text describes the press itself.
Bacon fat for tail fat in the Latin cookbook shows the northern fat world remaking an Arab dish.
The Thule hunters of the Arctic and the Basque whalers of Biscay are the two whale economies of the period, one for the household and one for the market.
The Fustat shop and the Egyptian flax and sesame economy are the retail end of the same oil trade.
The synagogue accounts of linseed oil are the consumer end of the Egyptian linseed economy.
The Tunisian merchant in Palermo and the skins of Tunisian oil reaching Egypt are the same Mediterranean oil trade.
The Borneo coconut-oil jars and Hangzhou’s oil among the seven necessities are two oil markets of the same century range.
The Yuan dietetics text and the Arab dishes in Latin cookbooks both carry the tail-fat cooking of the Muslim and Turkic worlds into a new court.
The tail fat of the Mongol court and the shift of su from butter to animal-fat shortening are two sides of Yuan China’s fat.
The Polynesian settlers and the Borneo coconut-oil jars are two Pacific coconut-and-nut economies of the same medieval centuries.
Polo’s sesame in Persia and India and the Song oil-lists that rank sesame best are two thirteenth-century views of the same crop.
Thule hunters’ Arctic blubber lamps and the Mitchell Site’s bone-grease station are two North American fat economies of the same centuries.
